name: an assistant's estimates and proposals are not facts
piece:
ai: No, 1M context is not enabled, and the numbers say it would cost about four times more per call. The chat runs Sonnet with the standard window and rolls a turn over to a fresh call at 150k tokens (`--rollover`, default 150000).

**What the optimal context is**

I fitted a cost model to the agent's last seven context segments. From the logs:
- a fresh call after a rollover starts at about 58k tokens;
- context then grows about 1,590 tokens per model call;
- a cached token costs a tenth of an uncached one to read, and a rollover re-reads its starting context uncached, with cache writes at up to twice the base price.

Cost per model call at different rollover thresholds, at list prices:

| roll over at | cost per call |
|---|---|
| 80k | $0.031 |
| 95k | $0.025 |
| 120k | $0.024 |
| 150k (now) | $0.025 |
| 200k | $0.028 |
| 400k | $0.047 |
| 1M | $0.106 |

- **The optimum is about 105–120k**, depending on which cache lifetime the provider bills.
- **The curve is flat there.** Today's 150k is only about 5% above the best, so tuning the threshold alone gains little.
- **Large contexts lose.** Every call re-reads the whole context, so cost climbs steadily past 200k.
- **Limits of the model.** It counts money only. It ignores that a rollover loses working detail (the agent may re-read files afterwards) and that responses get slower as context grows.

The bigger levers are the two inputs, not the threshold: the 58k a fresh call starts with, and the 1,590 tokens each call adds. Halving the restart size would lower the whole curve by more than any threshold change.

**Feedback control for when to compact**

Yes, and the chat already sees everything it needs in the per-call usage it records. I'd build it like the controller that tunes the compactor's line length:

1. **Estimate continuously** the restart size and the growth per call from the turn's own calls.
2. **Compute the threshold** from them: restart size plus the square root of (2 × write-to-read price ratio × restart size × growth), clamped to a sane range such as 80k–200k. When the agent is doing small reads it rolls later; when it is pulling in large outputs it rolls sooner.
3. **Roll when the cache has gone cold.** After a long tool call or a pause past the cache lifetime, the next call pays full price for the whole context anyway, so rolling over at that moment is nearly free. This would have applied after the 15-minute `bench` stall.
4. **Prefer natural boundaries.** Inside a window around the threshold, roll right after a commit or a green test rather than mid-edit, so less working detail is lost.
5. **Charge rollovers their real cost.** Count the calls spent re-reading files just after each rollover and add that to the rollover's price, so the controller backs off if rollovers turn out to hurt.

Items 3 and 4 are where I'd expect the real gain, since the pure threshold is already near its optimum.

I can queue this for the agent once its current round ends, along with a breakdown of what makes up the 58k restart. Do you want that?

name: what only a person at the command line does is the operator's
piece:
ai: You can now write to the running agent from `top`: press `i` in any non-pane tab, type the line, Enter sends it and Esc drops it.

- **From `top`:** the line you are writing shows on the bottom row, and once sent it appears in the history as a `user:` message, followed by the agent's reply.
- **From a shell or script:** `ghci-session chat --send 'a line' -s dxf` does the same.
- **When it is read:** between two tool calls if a turn is running, or as the next turn if the agent is idle.
- **Which chat gets it:** the last chat started on the session, whatever its standard input is. If you open the chat tab (`7`) in `top`, that new chat becomes the receiver instead of the DXF agent.

The TUI suite has a new check that types a line in `top` and sees the chat answer it (43 checks pass, self-tests 338). `chat --send` shares that code path but was not run on its own. This is committed and pushed on `top-and-chat-memory`, the README is updated, and the new binary is installed.

I hot-reloaded the DXF chat onto the new build so it listens to the inbox; it restarted cleanly and is idle, since its allocation turn has ended. I did not send it a test message because that would start a turn. The old `chat.in` pipe still works too.

The scroll fix from earlier had only been checked against the old `.bin` binary by the TUI suite; it has now been rebuilt and passes there as well.

name: an agent's report of work done and measured gives its results
piece:
talk: Both optimisation targets are met on f001.dxf, the largest sample (19.3 MB, 112,322 LINEs). The full check, `Check.runWith ""`, passes 37 of 37 checks. They compare all the samples with ezdxf and cover the round trip and the text/binary tag layer. Everything is committed on `full-parser` and nothing is pushed.

The aim for parse speed is met only on LINE-heavy files. The two small POLYLINE/TEXT samples parse at about 34 MB/s, below the 100 MB/s aim.

| f001 | before (54a1d27) | now | ezdxf |
|---|---|---|---|
| parse to typed document | 468 ms (47 MB/s) | 138 ms (140 MB/s) | 3.35 s |
| print | 704 ms | 85 ms (228 MB/s) | 3.65 s |
| max residency | 100 MB | 43 MB (2.2× the file) | n/a |
| peak RSS | 227 MB | 83 MB | 263 MB |

Printing is now faster than parsing. The two small samples show the same pattern as the table:

| sample | size | parse | print |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPQ-SPS-ZZ-ZZ-DR-A-0005 | 509 KB | 15 ms | 19 ms |
| condo_A-301_arch-elevation | 470 KB | 14 ms | 18 ms |

Both go through the slower general codecs for POLYLINE, VERTEX and TEXT.

What changed, in the order of the commits:
- **LINE decoder (078bcc4):** LINE is read straight from the source bytes, layer, owner and linetype strings are shared between neighbouring entities, and points are unpacked.
- **Double formatter (e9bc1cb):** doubles are written with a Grisu2 shortest-digits printer (`Tag/Double.hs`) straight into the output buffer.
- **Number reading and tag scanning (1e59861):** `readDouble` uses the Eisel-Lemire algorithm for long decimals, the group-code line is read in one pass, and `readDouble` no longer goes through Integer arithmetic.
- **Printing (e327ed2, 3ce585d, b61b6b7):** each text tag is written by one buffer primitive (`Tag/Prim.hs`), and the entity head is one primitive. A whole LINE, head plus six numbers, is one primitive (`Entity/FastOut.hs`).
- **Tests:** new checks cover `readDouble` rounding over 300,000 random decimals, `doubleText` read-back and shortest digits, fast decoder against general decoder, and the one-primitive LINE against the codecs in all eight layouts.
- **Fixture generator:** `tools/gen_binary.py` now writes the r12/r2007/r2018 text and binary fixtures, and `tools/gen_all.sh` runs it with the others. I deleted `r12.bin.dxf` and reran the script to confirm it comes back.
- **`PERF.md`:** it has a before/after table for each step, the profile findings, the ezdxf comparison and what is left.

What is left, also listed in `PERF.md`:
- **Other entity types:** VERTEX, LWPOLYLINE, TEXT, INSERT, CIRCLE and ARC still use the field-table codecs, which allocate a closure per field. The small samples parse and print below the aim because of this.
- **Source bytes for unchanged doubles:** I did not write doubles back from their source bytes. The printer produces shortest digits, which matches CAD output on the samples, and keeping the bytes would cost memory per number.
- **Slower re-parse:** the printed f001 parses in about 172 ms against about 140 ms for the original. I did not investigate why.

name: progress: a step done and pushed is a moment
piece:
ai: Step 1 is done and pushed: there is now one room finder in the modelling package, and House MM, Colchester and the intake all call it.

## What changed

- **New shared module `Examples.PlanRooms`** holds both existing ways of finding rooms, moved verbatim:
  - House MM's flood fill, for walls and openings that already close the rooms;
  - Colchester's version, which closes doorways by growing the barrier 0.55 m before filling, then grows each room back to the lines.
- **House MM and Colchester now import it** in place of their own copies.
- **The intake's plan tree uses it too.** The raster room code I wrote earlier today is deleted.

## Checks

- House MM: 22 of 22 goldens match, plus the rooms golden.
- Colchester: still 58 rooms, 50 named, and its snapshot still has 1,151 elements and 607 constraints. Colchester has no rooms golden, so this is a count check, not a byte comparison.
- Intake: the plan tree gives the same findings as before (a door spans a wall gap 70% of the time, furniture touches no wall 63%) and runs in 4.7 seconds, down from 28.

## Remaining steps

2. Generalise Colchester's context path into the shared engine, so a place can be a room as well as a grid cell, with wall-standing as a fact of the place.
3. Move the multi-source vote down, and add shape, size and wall-standing as sources.
4. Use Colchester's identified solids as the library's second office, labelled as things.

I'll carry on with step 2 unless you want a different order.

name: progress: a breakdown measured along the way
piece:
ai: Yes, the gaps can be fixed, but each needs a real reader, and the biggest one — the roof — is the most work. I measured where the elevations' missing lines actually are, tried the cheapest fix, and it did not help, so here is the evidence and a ranked plan.

## Where the elevations' "not built" is

Of about 1,800 m not built across the four elevations, by height:

| Height band | Not built | What is there |
|---|---|---|
| 9 m and above | about 720 m | roofs, parapets, tank housing |
| around 7 m | 264 m | probably balcony rails on the upper floor |
| around 1 m | 272 m | basement level: probably garden walls and the ramp |
| −1 to 0 m | about 190 m | ground and site |

By layer, 255 m of it is window and door linework (frames and mullions).

## What I tried just now

Parapets from the roof plan's low walls, standing on the roof slab. It found only 5 on House MM, 4 of them with no height readable, and the divergence rose by 7.5 m. I left them out of the model; the code is kept but switched off.

The reason it found so few is a classification gap: House MM's roof plan has 533 m of line on layer `0`, which nobody gave a role, so the intake ignores it. The same layer holds 1,350 m in the sections and elevations.

## The fixes, ranked

1. **Roofs (about 720 m).** Pitched roofs need the roof plan's ridge, hip and eave lines plus heights from the sections. House MM already has a reader for this; per your consolidation rule I'd move it down into the shared engine and drive it by layer role. This is the largest gain and the largest job.
2. **Window and door detail on facades (255 m).** House MM has a reader for mullions, transoms and frames from elevations. Same approach: move it down.
3. **Rails and garden walls (the 7 m and 1 m bands, about 530 m).** These are low walls and rails whose heights the side views show; an extension of what I built today.
4. **Layer `0`.** Decide what it is on the intake page, or let me look at what it draws. If it is real building linework, classifying it feeds items 1 and 3 directly.
5. **Ground (about 190 m).** Needs a site model; I'd leave it for last.

## Realistic expectation

House MM's hand-built model reached about 1,540 m after weeks of project-specific work. The intake is at 6,651 m. A generic pass through items 1 to 3 should bring that down substantially, but I would not expect it to reach House MM's figure without project-specific decisions.

The cheapest next step is item 4: I'll look at what layer `0` draws on the roof plan and elevations, which takes minutes and tells us whether the roof reader has enough to work with. Shall I start there?

name: progress: a change with its before/after
piece:
ai: The intake is now wired into the quick workflow and pushed, and I used it for a first real improvement: adding low walls brought House MM's divergence from 7,349 m to 7,189 m.

## The edit loop

In the `intake` session, point it at a project and use the same commands as House MM and Colchester:

- `quickBase` holds the baseline: 1,791 elements, 10 views and 3,862 divergences in 7.4 seconds.
- Edit how the model is built, reload, then `quickEdit` re-projects the ten views in 7.7 seconds and lists what is gone, new or moved.
- `quickViews`, `quickTotals`, `quickDivergences`, `quickRender`, `quickLines`, `quickAt` and `quickElement` come from the same engine but I have only run `quickViews` so far.

One difference from House MM: what you edit is a rule for building the model, not a single element, because the model-building code is shared by every intake project.

## First use: low walls

I summed the divergences by layer and kind to find what to build first. The largest "drawn but not built" items were:
- elevation lines: 1,117 m;
- things the plans draw above their cut: 676 m;
- the plans' low walls: 627 m, plus 258 m in elevations and 189 m in sections.

Low walls were the most direct to build: the same line-pairing as full walls, applied to the low-wall layer, at an assumed height of 1.10 m (flagged as assumed in each element).

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Total divergence | 7,349 m | 7,189 m |
| Plans | 2,105 m | 1,898 m |
| Side views | 5,244 m | 5,291 m |
| Drawn line within 5 cm of the model | 38% | 40% |

The plans improved by 207 m. The side views got 47 m worse, because 1.10 m is a guess and the drawings show these walls at other heights. Reading that height from the side views, the way window sills are read, is the natural fix.

## Practical note

A session started before this change needs a stop and start to pick up the new module; I did that for `intake`.

## Next candidates, by size of what's missing

1. Low-wall heights from the side views.
2. Slabs from the sections, replacing the assumed 12 cm under each room.
3. What plans draw above their cut (roof edges, overhangs), which needs the roof plan brought into the frame.

name: a finding that stands: licensing
piece:
ai: I downloaded a catalog and it gave the first cross-office result that beats guessing: with it in the library, House MM's windows are named correctly 85% of the time and its doors about 45%, where both were 0% before.

## What I downloaded

**FloorPlanCAD** is a research dataset of over 10,000 real CAD floor plans, cut into 10 × 10 m tiles as vector SVG. Every line is labelled with what it is and which instance it belongs to. The drawings come from many offices: the test set alone has 3,424 different layer names.

- I took the test set: 5,502 tiles, now in `data/catalogs/floorplancad/svg` (562 MB).
- `tools/intake/floorplancad.py` converts a sample into an intake project. I used every ninth tile: 612 tiles and 4,684 labelled things (894 single doors, 653 windows, 465 double doors, 452 chairs, 360 sinks, 178 toilets, 167 stairs, and more), each with the walls around it.

I also downloaded LibreCAD's small open symbol library (31 furniture and bathroom symbols plus 4 doors), but have not used it yet.

## Licence

FloorPlanCAD's annotations are Creative Commons non-commercial, and the authors state they do not own the copyright of the drawings. It is fine for research and for testing our method, but it cannot ship inside a product. LibreCAD's library is GPL-2.

## Results with the catalog in the library

House MM, named only from other offices' drawings:

| Kind | Before the catalog | With the catalog |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | 0% | 85% |
| Doors | 0% | 41–45% |
| Furniture | 40–85% | 50% |
| Fixtures | 22–26% | 0% |
| All features | 23% | 47% |

Always guessing House MM's commonest kind would score 42%. Context and length alone, without the shape tree, scored 56%.

Two things did not improve:
- **House MM's fixtures** went to 0%. I have not looked into why.
- **The SketchUp plans** stay below guessing (17–19%), consistent with their unclean walls and labels.

## What else it showed

- **The class numbers in the files are not the ones in the paper.** Read by the paper's list, "single door" came out as 322,869 lines and "window" as 124. I took the correct mapping from the dataset authors' own code and checked it against the layer names in the files (class 1 sits on WALL layers, class 30 on STAIR layers).
- **Scale checks out.** One unit is 0.1 m: a single door comes out at 0.88 m, a toilet at 0.70 × 0.48 m, a bed at 2.00 × 1.38 m.
- **Offices draw doors differently.** In this catalog doors touch no wall 41% of the time, because the swing is drawn out in the room. So the "both ends at walls, under 30 cm" rule is right 84% of the times it fires there, but finds only 28% of openings, against 82% on House MM. Windows span a gap 59% of the time.

## Practical notes

- The Mac's disk had only 2.5 GB free, so I deleted the 1.8 GB archive after extracting the SVGs. The download command is in the script's header.
- The three-project run takes about 2 minutes.

## Next

The obvious follow-ups are to use the full 5,502 tiles and the fine classes (toilet, sink, bed, stair), and to add a door rule for swings drawn in the room. Shall I go on with those?

Sources:
- [FloorPlanCAD dataset site](https://floorplancad.github.io/)
- [FloorPlanCAD paper (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.07147)
- [CADTransformer class mapping](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/VITA-Group/CADTransformer/main/config/anno_config.py)
- [LibreCAD part library](https://github.com/LibreCAD/LibreCAD)
- [CubiCasa5K (considered, not used)](https://github.com/cubicasa/cubicasa5k)
- [Voxel51 FloorPlanCAD mirror (raster only, not used)](https://docs.voxel51.com/dataset_zoo/datasets_hf/floorplancad.html)

name: a finding that stands: why a score is circular
piece:
ai: Tagging Colchester's plan copy did not help much, but it exposed something more important: House MM's scores for the fusion are partly circular. Committed and pushed.

**The tagging**
- The SketchUp plan copy has no layers, but each line belongs to a block, so I tagged by block name: furniture, fixtures, grid, boundary, roof, screens, doors.
- 6,021 of the 8,717 lines are in no block at all. That is where the walls are, mixed with everything else drawn loose.
- So the wall count stayed at 1,514 line pairs. I added a filter that drops lines that are part of a regular rhythm (stair treads, deck boards, screen slats); that took it to 1,058.
- Neither change moved the result: faces on a "wall" are on the model 54% of the time, faces on none 48%.

**What that led me to check**

Are the walls the intake reads from the plans actually in each model?

| | Walls from plans | Stand in the model's material | Both faces on model faces |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 Colchester Drive | 1,058 | 72% | 35% |
| House MM | 137 | 100% | 100% |

MM's 100% is because MM's model walls were built from the same pairing of the same plan lines. So the headline "a face on a wall the plans cut is 94% on the model" mostly says that a face on a plan wall is on a plan wall. The same applies, less completely, to slabs (MM's come from its sections) and to corners (MM's boxes are built from these drawings).

**What this means for the numbers I've reported**
- Every "on MM's model" figure from the fusion steps is optimistic, and the wall and slab tiers most of all.
- The only independent test is Colchester: corners 29%, edges 17%, faces about half, and no gain from walls.
- Colchester has its own handicaps: plans with no layers, and a model of SketchUp solids that is coarser than the drawings.
- The one result that holds on both projects is that about half the faces land on the model.

The mechanisms are all built and run. That they find the building better is not yet shown beyond that.

**A clean test needs both** plans with real layers and a model not built from them. Candidates: House 16FA or Schependomlaan (each has an IFC model and its own drawings), or Colchester if the floor-plan DWG that the tender set references can be obtained. Do you have that DWG, or should I look at what drawings exist for the other two?
